quote: a. Gegeben [-1-] Kreis im Raume, gesucht 1 zweideutiges räumliches Potential für welches der Kreis Verzweigungs- gebilde ist und in dem einen Raume an einer gegebenen Stelle unendlich wird.
english: a. Given a circle in space, find a two-valued spatial potential for which the circle is the branching locus and which becomes infinite at a given point in one of the spaces.
topic: A pasted-in list of potential-theory problems (a two-valued spatial potential with a circle as branch locus, a potential that equals +1 on one side of a disc and 0 on the other, and a proof of Appell's results), followed by a proof that a function annihilated by a product of difference operators in x and y must be a sum of polynomial-in-one-variable terms with coefficients depending on the other variable.

triage.modern_statement: Take a circle C in R^3 and build the two-sheeted Riemann space branched along C. Two sheets of R^3 are glued crosswise across the disc that C bounds, the way a Riemann surface is built for sqrt(z) but one dimension higher. On this space, find a harmonic function u (a 'Sommerfeld potential'). It must be single-valued on the double cover, branched only along C, and harmonic everywhere except at one prescribed point P on one sheet, where it has a 1/r singularity like a point charge. It should also be regular, with suitable decay, at infinity on both sheets. In other words, the problem asks for the fundamental solution (Green's function) of the Laplacian on the double cover of R^3 branched over a circle. This is a three-dimensional version of Appell's 1887 multivalued potentials, which were branched along a straight line.
triage.answered_by: Arnold Sommerfeld set up the general method in 'Über verzweigte Potentiale im Raum' (Proc. London Math. Soc. 28, 1896/97, pp. 395–429). He was working in Göttingen at the time, which is also where the paper is signed. E. W. Hobson then used Sommerfeld's method with a well-chosen coordinate system to construct the two-sheeted potential branched on a circle explicitly, and with it the Green's function of the circular disc: 'On Green's function for a circular disc, with applications to electrostatic problems', Trans. Cambridge Phil. Soc., 1900. The sources I found do not show whether Sommerfeld's 1897 paper already handled the circle case itself.

evidence.claim: Appell published 'Quelques remarques sur la théorie des potentiels multiformes' in Math. Ann. 30 (1887), 155–156. Its topic, multivalued potentials, matches the 'Appell's results' item on the same page of the diary.
A. von Sommerfeld (Göttingen) published 'Über verzweigte Potentiale im Raum' in Proc. London Math. Soc. s1-28, pp. 395–429.

Hobson used Sommerfeld's method and a clever choice of coordinates to find the Green function for an equipotential circular disc in 3D. In this picture the disc acts as a doorway between two copies of E_3, which is exactly the two-sheeted space branched on the circle.
Reference lists cite Hobson, E. W. (1900), 'On Green's function for a circular disc, with applications to electrostatic problems', as the application of Sommerfeld's method to the circular disc.
Sommerfeld's branched-potential (image) method is still used in recent work. For example, Green functions for grounded circular and elliptical rings and hyperspheres were built this way in 2018–2019.

triage.why: The note asks for the Green's function of the Laplacian on the double cover of space branched along a circle. Sommerfeld's 1897 theory of branched potentials covers this kind of problem, and Hobson solved the circle case explicitly in 1900. The disc problem on the same page (+1 on one side, 0 on the other) belongs to the same family. The problem is not among Hilbert's 23 problems or his 24th problem. It is now classical: the method still shows up in electrostatics and diffraction papers, but the question itself is not an open research topic. Confidence is medium for three reasons. I could not confirm that Hilbert's note directly led to Sommerfeld's work, though both were in Göttingen at the time. I am not sure the problem was first solved by Sommerfeld rather than Hobson. And I could not check the exact boundary and normalisation conditions Hilbert had in mind.
